                                                        Learning to Assist: Physics-Grounded Human-Human Control
                                                                  via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

                                         Figure 1. AssistMimic: We propose a multi-agent RL framework capable of learning robust Supporter and Recipient policies from noisy,
                                         close-proximity motion sequences. By leveraging single-person motion priors, a novel recipient-adaptive reference retargeting mechanism,
                                         and contact-promoting rewards, AssistMimic becomes the first physics-based controller to successfully track such complex, high-contact
                                         reference motions. Snapshots are arranged chronologically from left to right.

extending it with partner-aware state inputs and augmenting standard imitation rewards with recipient-aware reference retargeting and

                                                                                         5. Conclusion
As shown in Table 3, AssistMimic exhibits strong robust-
ness to unseen recipient constraints. Removing the contact                               We introduced AssistMimic, a multi-agent reinforcement
reward or dynamic reference retargeting substantially de-                                learning framework for learning physics-aware, tracking
grades this robustness, suggesting that encouraging deliber-                             controllers that reproduce and adapt to human–human in-
ate contacts during RL enables the policy to acquire diverse                             teractions, including assistive behaviors. Unlike prior ap-
support strategies. Consequently, it handles changes in re-                              proaches that treat interaction partners independently or
cipient limitations, such as unexpected stumbles or altered                              rely on fixed replayed trajectories, AssistMimic jointly
load distributions, with high accuracy.                                                  learns policies for both agents, enabling reactive and phys-
                                                                                         ically consistent coordination. AssistMimic improves ex-
4.4. Tracking of Generated Interactions
                                                                                         ploration and stability in RL through three key innovations:
Figure 6 illustrates the results of applying AssistMimic to                              (1) weight initialization from single-human tracking con-
trajectories synthesized by a text-conditioned motion dif-                               trollers, which stabilizes early learning; (2) dynamic refer-
fusion model [25] (details in Appendix F). The diffusion                                 ence retargeting, allowing the policy to adjust to the recip-
model was trained on ”Help-up” interactions from the Inter-                              ient’s current pose; and (3) contact-promoting rewards, en-
X dataset. During inference, we prompt it with unseen                                    couraging physically meaningful interactions. Experiments
text descriptions from the same category. While the gener-                               on the Inter-X and HHI-Assist show that AssistMimic is the
ated kinematics capture the interaction semantics, they of-                              first method capable of successfully tracking assistive inter-
ten contain physical artifacts such as foot sliding and pen-                             action sequences. More broadly, our results demonstrate a
etration. AssistMimic successfully converts dense interac-                               generalizable framework for extending single-agent imita-
tion kinematics into physically plausible motions. This re-                              tion learning to physically grounded multi-agent domains,
sult demonstrates that AssistMimic is effective not only for                             with promising implications for assistive robotics, collabo-
real interaction data but also for generated data, highlight-                            rative manipulation, and embodied simulation of social in-
ing its generality and broad applicability.                                              teractions.

F.3. Model architecture
Our implementation of the diffusion planner G is based on
MDM [25]. It is trained to predict the clean motion win-
dow x̂i:i+N
       0     from a noisy version xi:i+N
                                    t    , conditioned on
the previous window and the text embedding. The diffusion
timestep is denoted by t:

          x̂i:i+N = G xi:i+N , t, xi−N :i , ztext .
                                                 
            0          t


   During training, the windows xi−N :i and xi:i+N t      are
concatenated and processed with self-attention, while the
text embedding is incorporated via cross-attention in the
transformer decoder layers. The motion windows along
with the text embedding are all projected to the same latent
dimension to be compatible with the attention layers.
   We optimize the standard Lsimple loss together with a loss
for temporal consistency Lvel , weighted by λvel = 25:

               N −1
           1 X                                       2
                          xi+1 − xi0 − x̂0i+1 − x̂0i 2 .
                                    
  Lvel =                   0
         N − 1 i=1


                  L = Lsimple + λvel Lvel .

   Specifically, our model uses a transformer decoder with
10 layers and 8 attention heads, a feedforward dimension of
2048, and a latent dimension of 768, with dropout set to 0.1.
The prediction window is N = 20 frames. During training,
the conditioning variables are masked with a probability of
0.1 to enable unconditional generation. The diffusion pro-
cess uses 100 timesteps with a cosine beta schedule. We
optimize the model using AdamW with a learning rate of
2 × 10−4 , betas (0.9, 0.95), and weight decay 10−3 . Train-
ing is performed for 8 hours on an NVIDIA A6000 GPU.
